This research introduces a dynamic generalization of Poisson autoregressive models, allowing for time-varying parameters and external influences, to better capture the complexities of real-time series data. Unlike traditional Poisson AR models that assume constant parameters, our model employs a state space framework with a Kalman filter smoother to estimate dynamic parameters and external effects, even in the presence of non-stationarity. We demonstrate the efficacy of this model by applying it to simulate and analyze real-world data sets, including a simulation study and case studies involving crime statistics and sports data. The model's performance is compared to static Poisson AR and negative binomial generalized autoregressive conditional distributions methods, revealing its superiority in capturing non-linear dynamics and external influences. The research also explores the relationship between the model's components and provides a user-friendly R package, tvpar, for estimating and analyzing time-varying parameters in Poisson autoregressive models.

Reaching for objects in cluttered environments is a fundamental task for robots, and it is heavily influenced by the 3D pose estimation of objects. To achieve this, researchers have been exploring methods that utilize convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to directly estimate pose parameters from single images. However, this approach is challenging due to the high dimensionality of pose parameters and the limited amount of training data available for many object classes. To address this issue, we propose a novel method called DeepHMap++ that combines projection grouping and correspondence learning to estimate the 6-DoF pose of objects from a single RGB image. In this approach, a CNN is used to predict a set of 2D projection maps, and a separate network is employed to establish correspondences between the predicted maps and the image features. The correspondences are then used to calculate the 6-DoF pose parameters. We tested our method on the BOP dataset and achieved state-of-the-art results. Additionally, we applied our method to estimate the pose of a real object in a cluttered environment using a robotic arm. The code for DeepHMap++ is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yang/DeepHMap++.systemassistant

Multilingual individuals frequently switch between languages when communicating, resulting in code-mixed text that combines elements from two or more languages within a single utterance. This phenomenon is particularly prevalent in regions with multiple dominant languages, such as South Asia, where code-mixed speech and writing are common in social media, online forums, and everyday conversations. Code-mixed language poses significant challenges for natural language processing tasks, including classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation, due to its inherent hybrid nature, which blends syntax, vocabulary, and semantics from the involved languages. As a result, researchers and practitioners in the field of NLP are faced with multiple obstacles, including determining the best approach to preprocess code-mixed data, selecting suitable models, and evaluating their performance, as well as addressing broader societal issues, such as inequality and social exclusion, that underlie the use of code-mixed language. This paper delves into the intricacies of code-mixed NLP, exploring its challenges, potential applications, and societal implications, and highlights areas of ongoing research, including multimodal analysis, transfer learning, and multimodal learning, as well as the role of code-mixed language in reflecting and shaping societal dynamics. Through this, we aim to foster collaboration and knowledge sharing among researchers from various disciplines, including linguistics, sociology, and computer science, to tackle the complex challenges associated with code-mixed NLP and its broader societal implications. This paper is an expanded version of the abstract submitted to the workshop on Multilingualism in NLP for Multilingual Societies, held in conjunction with the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics.

However, when these descriptions are compared to human-generated descriptions
based on references, they can provide valuable insights into the system's
abilities. We propose a method to assess the value of such references in an
uncontrolled setting by utilizing a set of reference descriptions that were
created by multiple people. This method allows us to determine whether human
descriptions generated automatically are more effective at matching the most
popular references than they would be in a real-world scenario. We applied
this method to a well-known dataset and found that the system's performance
could be improved by being more selective in its descriptions. We also found
that the system's ability to match the most popular references varied
significantly depending on the image, and that this variation was not
explained by any of the features we examined. We believe that this method can
be applied to other evaluation tasks involving human-generated descriptions.

Conversational interfaces are becoming increasingly prevalent, and the demand for reliable and user-friendly interfaces is driving the need for rigorous testing of these systems. However, testing conversational agents poses a significant challenge due to the open-ended nature of user input and the lack of a clear success metric. In response, we propose a novel automated testing framework that leverages reinforcement learning to evaluate the effectiveness of conversational agents. This framework enables the creation of test cases that mimic real user interactions and assess the agents' ability to achieve desired outcomes. By utilizing a simple and efficient reward function, our framework can effectively evaluate the performance of conversational agents in a range of scenarios. We have applied our framework to evaluate the performance of a state-of-the-art conversational agent on a real-world task, demonstrating its practical utility. The proposed framework is also adaptable to accommodate various performance metrics and user preferences, making it a valuable tool for developers and researchers seeking to assess and improve the performance of conversational agents. The framework's code is available online for public use.

Cross-domain recommendation has been widely used in various applications, and it has been particularly successful in multi-sparse-domain scenarios. However, existing methods often rely on explicit domain transfer or assume that domains share similar features, which can be impractical in real-world scenarios. In contrast, we propose a novel approach called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation via Enhanced Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (MSD-CARE), which leverages the inherent differences between domains without explicit transfer. MSD-CARE extracts a comprehensive set of aspects from multiple sparse domains and learns a unified preference matrix to make recommendations. We evaluate our approach on three real-world datasets and compare it to multiple state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth analysis of MSD-CARE's components and provide actionable guidelines for practitioners. Our approach and experimental results indicate that learning a unified preference matrix is crucial for cross-domain recommendation, and MSD-CARE achieves superior performance by capturing the intrinsic differences between domains. We also release our code and datasets for public use.

Finally, we outline the implications of our findings for the theory of closed orbits in Hamiltonian systems.

This approach enables us to efficiently create a wide array of modified gravity simulations, which can be used to isolate the effects of different gravity theories and assess their impact on cosmic large-scale structures. By applying a set of predefined criteria, we've determined the most suitable simulations for various research applications and made them available for public use. These simulations can be used in conjunction with various observational datasets to test the validity of modified gravity theories and to create mock galaxy distributions for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. We've also developed a set of rapid N-body simulations for the $\Lambda$CDM model, which can be used as a reference for comparing the effects of modified gravity on galaxy distributions. This integrated analysis reveals that certain genomic elements are associated with multiple traits, and these elements tend to be located in gene-rich regions, near active genes, and are characterized by specific histone modification marks. Furthermore, we develop a method to prioritize associations based on their enrichment within specific genomic elements, and apply this to identify key elements associated with multiple traits. Our findings demonstrate that this approach can pinpoint the genomic elements responsible for the majority of trait-associated variation, with up to 70% of trait-associated variation explained by a small subset of elements. This study provides a framework for large-scale integrated analysis of GWAS and functional genomics data, and highlights the importance of considering the broader genomic context when interpreting the biological relevance of genetic variants associated with complex traits. Our findings show that HNNs can successfully learn the dynamics of these processes and accurately forecast their gradients, surpassing the performance of traditional neural network-based predictors. This study focuses on key aspects in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing: handling schema links and incorporating world knowledge. To address these challenges, we propose a hybrid approach that combines two parsing pathways: a primary path for executing the SQL query and a secondary path for predicting the schema links and relevant spans. This approach is supported by an auxiliary task that generates a pseudo-document related to the query, and we demonstrate that this auxiliary task is beneficial for enhancing the parser's performance. To further improve the parser, we introduce a schema link prediction sub-task and a span prediction sub-task in the primary path. Our proposed method, a hybrid parser, is evaluated on the Spider dataset and achieves a 5.1% execution accuracy improvement and a 7.5% total success rate improvement over the baseline model. However, the inherent randomness in many algorithms introduces significant variance, making it difficult to accurately determine the best hyperparameters. This issue is particularly pronounced when using grid search to find the optimal hyperparameters, and the resulting models exhibit poor generalizability due to an overemphasis on models that perform well on the training set but poorly on new data. To mitigate this problem, researchers have proposed using K-fold cross-validation to evaluate the quality of models, but this method can be computationally expensive and may not effectively reduce the variance when selecting hyperparameters. In contrast, we propose using the J-K fold cross-validation method, which combines the efficiency of grid search with the variance reduction benefits of cross-validation. This method divides the data into K subsets, trains a model on a subset of the hyperparameters space, and then evaluates the model on the remaining data. This process is repeated by shifting the subset of hyperparameters by J steps, allowing the model to be evaluated on the entire hyperparameters space with a significant reduction in computational costs. Reconstructing 3D scenes from monocular images is a complex task, and estimating the motion between frames is crucial for achieving this goal. Self-supervised learning has been a successful approach for this estimation, but it relies heavily on the metric learning loss being accurate. However, our research reveals that this assumption is not necessarily true. We discovered that the metric loss can be manipulated to mislead the network, and this vulnerability can be leveraged to enhance self-supervised scene flow estimation. By introducing an adversarial loss that deceives the network about the scene flow, we developed a novel framework that combines this adversarial loss with a Pseudo-Point Cloud loss to estimate 3D scenes from monocular images in an end-to-end manner. This method surpasses the current state-of-the-art self-supervised scene flow estimation techniques and also achieves comparable results to supervised methods. Additionally, we demonstrated that this approach can be applied to other tasks, such as monocular depth estimation and 3D object detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-ai/AdMM.

A perfect matching in a graph is a set of edges without common vertices. We investigate graphs where every perfect matching can be mapped to a perfect 1-factorization, enabling the decomposition of all edges into perfect matchings, ultimately resulting in a Hamiltonian cycle. We establish a key condition for graphs with this property, demonstrating that every edge can be coloured with three different colours such that any two adjacent edges have different colours. We then develop a method for constructing an infinite family of graphs that satisfy this condition, providing a counterexample to a conjecture made by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza. We also examine the relationship between these graphs and those with a perfect 1-factorisation. Furthermore, we establish a connection between these graphs and the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle in the graph's edge-colouring configuration, ultimately leading to a result on the Hamiltonian cycle's length. We conclude by proposing several related questions for future exploration.

Modern cloud-native applications comprise numerous interconnected microservices, each with its own process, frequently interacting across the network. As a result, isolating individual services while maintaining inter-service communication poses a significant challenge. Traditional Linux Security Modules (LSMs) rely on complex rule sets to govern system calls, but they become unwieldy in the face of large, dynamic service landscapes. In contrast, our Timeloops system leverages machine learning to automate system call policies for containerized microservices, eliminating the need for manual configuration. By analyzing system logs and network traffic, Timeloops generates an efficient policy framework that restricts system calls and enables inter-service communication, all without disrupting the services themselves. Our experiments with real-world applications demonstrate a substantial reduction in policy complexity and comparable performance to manual configuration. Furthermore, we have made the Timeloops code available on GitHub under the Apache License 2.0.

This new paradigm offers multiple benefits, including enhanced data transmission rates, increased energy efficiency, and reduced heat generation. However, it introduces new sources of interference, complicating resource allocation and management. In this paper, we investigate the power allocation and scheduling problem in a hybrid integrated data and energy transmission network with D2D coexistence. We develop a new algorithm to solve the problem and evaluate its performance through simulations. Furthermore, we explore the impact of various parameters on the network's energy efficiency and data transmission rates. Additionally, we discuss the challenges and opportunities in this new paradigm and propose potential research directions. Finally, we present a hybrid integrated data and energy transmission network testbed and discuss its design and implementation. This work provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of research in this field and offers insights into the challenges and opportunities in this new paradigm. This leads to the discovery that first-order logic over infinite sequences with the successor function is equivalent to a specific class of functions defined by regular right-hand side transformations, and does not have the same expressive power as two-variable first-order logic over finite words. Furthermore, we establish the complexity of the synthesis problem for these functions as NP-complete, and provide a polynomial-time solution for a restricted version. Additionally, we show that first-order logic over finite words can be translated into a form of the sequence function using a data-word approach, and demonstrate the applicability of this translation to the synthesis of functions for infinite sequences. This is achieved by incorporating additional input symbols into the data words. This allows us to generalize the original problem to the synthesis of functions for finite words, and provide a characterization of first-order logic over finite words as the set of functions that map two data words to a third data word under the SCMG grammar. This characterization is then used to derive a new proof for the equivalence between first-order logic over finite words and regular right-hand side transformations. This involves a non-trivial generalization of the original proof, and provides a new perspective on the relationship between these two forms of logic. In this study, we demonstrate that multiple coexisting attractors can be beneficial for a deep neural network tasked with solving a classification problem. When a language model is transferred to a new task without explicit training data, it can leverage prior knowledge from a similar task it has been trained on. This phenomenon, known as cross-task generalization, can be facilitated by selecting tasks with overlapping data or similar language usage. However, there are many scenarios where suitable tasks are not readily available, and the model must rely on its inherent capacity for generalization. In this research, we explore unsupervised methods for facilitating cross-task generalization, focusing on transfer to classification tasks from a source conversation summarization task. We investigated three approaches to promote generalization: (1) using a contrastive diversity regularizer, (2) manipulating the model's input to prompt generalization, and (3) retrieving relevant conversation data to augment the model. Our findings show that retrieving relevant conversation data yields the best results, with an improvement of 4.5% in accuracy when transferring to a classification task with a 20% overlap in vocabulary, and 2.5% when transferring to a classification task with a 10% overlap in vocabulary. Our method for retrieving relevant conversation data also outperforms baselines that use pre-trained models for zero-shot transfer and few-shot learning. Our research provides a framework for evaluating unsupervised cross-task generalization and offers practical advice for applying it to real-world problems. Stream processing engines are designed to handle continuous data streams efficiently, and several systems have been developed to achieve high performance in this context. However, most existing research focuses on handling aperiodic or semi-structured data streams, with limited consideration for periodic data streams commonly found in time series applications. In contrast, periodic streams are ubiquitous in finance, weather forecasting, and sensor readings, and are often used in statistical analysis and machine learning. To address this gap, we present LifeStream, a high-performance stream processing engine specifically optimized for periodic data streams. LifeStream employs a novel scheduling approach that leverages the periodic nature of input streams to minimize overhead and ensure efficient processing. We evaluate LifeStream's performance using real-world datasets and find that it outperforms Apache Flink by up to 4.5x in throughput and 2.5x in latency. Additionally, LifeStream's scheduling strategy allows it to handle large-scale applications with a high level of concurrency. We also provide insights into LifeStream's design and discuss its limitations, as well as potential avenues for future research. System implementation and evaluation results are available at https://www.cse.ust.hk/~yjxu/projects/lifestream.

To tackle this issue, researchers have resorted to training models on vast amounts of text data, yet the lack of a well-defined evaluation framework has hindered progress. To address this limitation, we present ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas of machine commonsense consisting of 150,000 annotated statements that convey causal relationships between elements in a scene. This atlas is characterized by a nuanced understanding of causality, encompassing 20 distinct categories of relationships, and is grounded in a rich set of descriptive attributes that capture the nuances of a situation. To facilitate the utilization of this atlas, we introduce a suite of evaluation protocols that assess a model's capacity to reason about the world, evaluate its ability to generate coherent text, and explore the connection between text generation and reasoning. By leveraging this atlas, we demonstrate substantial improvements in the performance of state-of-the-art models on tasks such as abductive and deductive reasoning, as well as natural language generation. The comprehensive atlas of machine commonsense, along with the evaluation protocols and data, is available at https://atic.org.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in $b$-quark processes at the TeV scale, focusing on Drell-Yan dilepton production in proton-proton collisions. We develop an implementation for the next-to-leading order plus partonic shower accuracy in QCD using the Sherpa event generator, and apply it to study the impact of third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks on this process. We also examine the effects of these leptoquarks on associated production processes for top quarks and $b$-quarks in final states with same-flavour leptons. Our results demonstrate the importance of NLO corrections for these processes, particularly in the region of large dilepton invariant masses. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the production of dilepton pairs and the processes involving top quarks and $b$-quarks, and discuss the potential for future experiments to distinguish between different lepton-flavour universality violating scenarios. Our findings are applicable to the LHC at 13 TeV and 14 TeV, as well as future colliders like the High-Luminosity LHC and 100 TeV hadron colliders. Our event generator implementation can be used to simulate these processes for various leptoquark masses, and includes the simulation of detector effects and statistical analysis for the TeV scale. Our results are particularly relevant for the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC. Deep learning-based reconstruction techniques have significantly improved
image quality in PET scans, but they often require high-dose reference scans
for training, which is not ideal due to increased radiation exposure for
patients. To address this challenge, we developed a novel uncertainty-aware
deep learning framework that leverages low-dose and reference PET scans as
inputs. This approach employs a dual-resolution network with a coarse-scale
branch to generate a dense skip connection, enabling the refinement network
to focus on boundary and low-intensity regions. To evaluate our method's
performance, we conducted experiments using phantom and patient data sets. To
ensure robustness, we tested our approach on unseen data distributions, first
with phantom data and then with patient data from a different site. Our study
demonstrates that the proposed framework can effectively reduce PET scan doses to
1/5th the original amount without compromising image quality. Moreover, our
method's performance remains consistent even when applied to unseen data, without
requiring additional training. To facilitate further research, we have made our
code publicly available. To support clinical adoption, we have also conducted
statistical analysis to validate our method's performance on patient data sets.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. The minimum sized subset R that fully identifies the graph is known as its minimum identifying set, and the minimum sized subset R that fully identifies the graph where each vertex in R can determine all others by a unique sum of distances is known as the metric dimension of the graph. In contrast, the truncated version of the problem involves finding the minimum sized subset R of vertices where each vertex can determine all others by a unique sum of distances to at least one point in R, and no isolated point exists. This paper explores various properties of the Truncated Metric Dimension, provides a lower and upper bound for its value in graphs of n vertices, and proves that the Truncated Metric Dimension is equal to the metric dimension for trees, outdoes the metric dimension in some specific cases, and remains unknown for hypercubes. Additionally, the paper delves into a real-world application of the Trounded Metric Dimension in locating sensors within a network. Lastly, the paper offers two approaches to find the Truncated Metric Dimension of a graph: one algorithmic method and another that leverages the existing knowledge of the graph's metric dimension. The paper in conclusion highlights the numerous unanswered questions surrounding the Truncated Metric Dimension.

To address the issue of biased language models by creating counterfactual data, we propose a method called Discriminative Counterfactual Training (DCT) that generates phrasal counterfactuals. This approach is effective in producing high-quality data that can be used to train more equitable language models. However, it has limitations due to the high computational costs associated with training large-scale language models using DCT. To overcome this challenge, we developed a strategy called Distilling Counterfactuals with Large Language Models (DISCO. This method involves an initial training of a small counterfactual model, which is then used to generate a substantial amount of phrasal counterfactual data at a lower cost. This data is then utilized to fine-tune a large pre-trained language model through few-shot counterfactual distillation. Our findings demonstrate that DISCO is a cost-efficient and effective method for producing high-quality counterfactual data, which can be used to train language models that generalize well to new, unseen situations and exhibit improved performance in various tasks. Our approach also outperforms alternative methods for training large language models on multiple benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/nyuclsp/Disco.

Deep neural networks have achieved outstanding performance in image classification tasks, 
yet they struggle with multi-label classification problems where an image can have numerous 
relevant labels.  This issue stems from the limited supervision in standard single-label 
training datasets.  To address this limitation, we introduce a new method called Cross- 
Task Augmentation (CTA) to generate additional multi-label training samples from single 
positive label annotations.  CTA leverages the existing single-label classification model 
to predict a probability distribution over all possible labels, then selects the top N 
probabilistically most likely labels to create a new multi-label sample.  We demonstrate 
that using CTA-generated samples can significantly improve the performance of deep neural 
networks on multi-label classification tasks, and that this improvement is particularly 
pronounced when the number of possible labels is large.  We also show that CTA can be 
effectively used in conjunction with other data augmentation techniques to further 
boost performance.  Our code is available at https://github.com/chenxiwei0826/CTA.  Our 
experiments on the PASCAL VOC 2007 and ILSVRC 2010 multi-label classification datasets 
demonstrate that CTA can be an efficient and effective method for training deep neural 
networks on large-scale multi-label classification tasks with limited supervision.  We 
further investigate the relationship between the number of generated labels and the 
performance of deep neural networks, and find that there is an optimal number of 
generated labels that maximizes performance.  We also explore the application of CTA to 
single-class classification tasks, and find that it can be an effective method for 
training deep neural networks on these tasks with limited positive class examples.  We 
believe that CTA can be a valuable tool for training deep neural networks on a wide 
range of classification tasks with limited supervision.  We propose a new method called

The sequence reconstruction problem involves determining a sequence from
observations of its peers, where each peer represents a corrupted version of
the sequence, and the nature of the corruption is known. This problem has been
examined in various contexts, including combinatorial geometry, coding
theory, and statistical genetics, with applications in DNA sequence assembly
and image processing. In this study, we focus on reconstructing sequences of
permutations based on the Hamming distance, and we develop a set of criteria
to ensure the uniqueness of the solution, as well as estimates for the size
of the observation set required to guarantee a unique solution. Additionally,
we investigate the relationship between the size of the observation set and
the number of its maximal elements, and we provide a lower bound for the
minimum number of observations needed to reconstruct a sequence of
permutations with a given length. Furthermore, we examine the conditions
under which multiple solutions may arise, and we propose a method to
determine the number of distinct solutions from a given set of observations.

The team developed an efficient method to calculate the effects of eccentric binaries on gravitational waves for PTA observations, taking into consideration the movement of the Earth and the Sun. Additionally, they optimized the method to make it computationally feasible for large-scale PTA data analysis. Furthermore, they identified the most significant factors contributing to the PTA signal caused by eccentric binaries, which includes the rate of change of the gravitational wave frequency, the rate of change of the eccentricity, and the rate of change of the orbital phase. They also introduced a new method to calculate the time derivative of the orbital phase, which is essential for determining the orientation of the binary's elliptical orbit. They compared their method to existing approaches and found it to be more accurate and efficient. Finally, they made their code publicly available for further development and testing.

Instead, a neural network is utilized to directly compute the flux functions, allowing for an explicit and implicit solution approach for the advection and diffusion/gravitation terms respectively. This results in a significant reduction in computational time, with the proposed method demonstrating a 2.5 times increase in speed for an explicit approach and a 4.5 times boost for an implicit approach when compared to traditional numerical methods. Furthermore, the proposed method maintains stability and conservation properties, and can be applied to complex geometries with the use of a Cartesian cut cell method. As continuous learning becomes a necessity in complex and dynamic environments, the field of reinforcement learning has seen significant advancements. To evaluate the performance of lifelong reinforcement learning algorithms, a controlled assessment environment is crucial. However, existing assessment tools have limitations, such as focusing solely on single-task reinforcement learning evaluations or lacking the ability to dynamically change environments. In response to these challenges, we introduce L2Explorer, a comprehensive assessment platform that simulates various lifelong reinforcement learning scenarios. This environment features multiple learning tasks, each with its own set of parameters, and allows for seamless transitions between tasks. We demonstrate the versatility of L2Explorer by incorporating multiple benchmark problems, including a novel "parking" problem, and provide detailed instructions for modifying existing problems to suit the environment's requirements. The rapid spread of COVID-19 has put a significant burden on healthcare systems worldwide. To combat this, it's crucial to identify patients who require intensive care unit (ICU) admission early on. To facilitate the application of our method in clinical settings, we developed a user-friendly web platform for easy integration into existing healthcare systems. Our findings suggest that machine learning models can be effectively trained to predict ICU admission from X-ray images, providing a valuable tool for healthcare professionals in the fight against COVID-19. The task of identifying relationships between objects in images has significant potential for practical applications, yet the current state of the art is hindered by a major issue: the overwhelming majority of detected relationships are incorrect. To address this challenge, researchers have been experimenting with an unsupervised approach to model object relationships using deep neural networks. However, the method's limitations stem from its reliance on a large number of negative relationship predictions, which are often inaccurate. To make this task more feasible, it's essential to develop a more efficient way to predict object relationships. In this study, we propose a novel end-to-end supervised approach called Dual Path Network, which simultaneously identifies objects and models their relationships using a single network. The model's relationship prediction component is designed to minimize the number of negative predictions required, thereby significantly reducing false positives. To evaluate our method, we created a new dataset with precise labels for object relationships, and it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on two widely used benchmarks: Visual Genome and Foggy Visual Genome. In this research, we introduce a novel co-imitation learning framework that leverages the collective knowledge of multiple agents, each possessing unique skills, to accelerate learning without relying on expert demonstrations. The analysis of near-ultraviolet spectra during intense stellar flares can provide valuable insights into the physical processes driving the emission. This study's findings are relevant to the ongoing search for superflare stars with strong near-ultraviolet continuum in the spectra of giant flares. Additionally, the analysis of such continua can provide a new indicator for superflare stars, which may be particularly susceptible to extreme solar-like eruptions. Neural generative text models have gained significant attention in recent years, particularly in natural language processing tasks. Current methods rely heavily on word embeddings, which can be computationally expensive and require substantial memory for large vocabulary sizes. To address this challenge, a sparse generative model is proposed that utilizes a novel adversarial training framework to learn a compact, low-rank representation of words. This representation is characterized by a sparse distribution of latent codes, which are used to reconstruct language models via a non-autoregressive process. The proposed SparseGAN model leverages a dual adversarial training mechanism to learn this representation, ensuring that the generated codes conform to the same distribution as genuine codes. Experimental evaluations on multiple text generation tasks demonstrate the efficacy of the SparseGAN model, achieving superior results compared to conventional methods while utilizing a significantly reduced vocabulary size. The model's efficiency is further exemplified by a 98% reduction in vocabulary size for the 1000 most frequent words in the Wikipedia dataset. The code for the SparseGAN model is available at https://github.com/zhengyunwi/SparseGAN.

Genetic algorithms are then applied to adjust the material's geometry to optimize the distribution of damage within the composite, as visualized through the EIT images, by minimizing the difference between the simulated resistance patterns and the actual resistance distribution detected by the composite. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through numerical simulations of composite laminates, where the genetic algorithm successfully shapes the damage distribution by adjusting the fiber orientation to match the detected resistance patterns. The accuracy of the method is further validated through a comparison with an alternative optimization approach, demonstrating the genetic algorithm's ability to achieve precise control over damage development within composite materials. Understanding the intricate relationships within complex neural systems is a fundamental aspect of neuroscience research. Recent advancements in neuroimaging technologies have enabled the non-invasive assessment of neural interactions, which can be represented as directed connections within a graph. This graph is known as a directed functional connectivity (DFC) matrix, and its dynamic properties are crucial for comprehending the systems' temporal behavior. However, estimating DFC accurately is a challenging task due to the high dimensionality of neural data and the need for precise time-series alignment. In this study, we introduce a novel approach called Deep Dynamic Effective Connectivity Estimation (DDECE) via Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), which leverages the capabilities of recurrent neural networks and graph convolutional networks to model high-dimensional time-series data and graph dynamics simultaneously. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DDECE-GCN in capturing the non-stationarity of neural interactions using synthetic data and two empirical examples: a simulated neural mass model and resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project. The results show that DDECE-GCN accurately estimates the time-varying effective connectivity of complex neural systems, even in the presence of non-stationarity and non-sparse connections. To effectively address open-domain question answering without the need for a specific context, it is crucial to incorporate relevant semantic knowledge. However, the challenge lies in identifying the most suitable knowledge that directly addresses the question. In this work, we propose a novel approach to select relevant knowledge by leveraging a semantic similarity metric to prioritize knowledge with a high degree of relevance to the question. We utilize a knowledge graph as the source of semantic knowledge and develop a method to extract relevant knowledge based on the similarity between knowledge entities and the question. We evaluate our approach on the CommonsenseQA dataset and achieve a 4.3% improvement in F1-score compared to a strong baseline. We also conduct an ablation study to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in selecting the most relevant knowledge. Our approach ranks among the top 10% of submissions to the CommonsenseQA Challenge. We make our code publicly available.

In the context of semi-supervised image segmentation, a common challenge arises when there is a significant disparity between the amount of annotated training data and its unlabeled counterpart. To address this issue, various methods have been proposed that incorporate unannotated images through regularization techniques. However, these methods often rely on complex graph-based or self-supervised learning techniques that are computationally intensive and difficult to implement. In contrast, this study presents a straightforward and efficient method for training a single segmentation model using a consistency regularization loss function. This simple approach leverages unlabeled images to enforce spatial consistency in segmentations produced by the model, without the need for peer models or additional training. We evaluate our method on three benchmark datasets: ACDC, PROSTATE, and Brain Tumour Segmentation (BraTS). The results show that our simple approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods, while significantly reducing computational requirements. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/semi-supervised-seg.

We derive anisotropic relativistic stellar models for a two-fluid system with separate pressure contributions from each fluid component. The model's anisotropy parameter is determined by the difference between the radial pressure of the combined fluid and the radial pressure of an isotropic system with the same mass-energy distribution. Subsequently, an expression for the compactness of the star is obtained in terms of the anisotropy parameter, and we also examine the conditions under which the anisotropy parameter remains bounded within the star's interior. Furthermore, we investigate the stability of the star by analyzing the sign of the anisotropy parameter's derivative with respect to the compactness. Additionally, we derive anisotropic solutions for a specific two-fluid configuration, where the pressure of one fluid is directly proportional to the pressure of the other fluid. Finally, we provide anisotropic solutions for a static, spherically symmetric fluid distribution in General Relativity, where the pressure is proportional to the radial distance from the center of the star. These solutions can be applied to various astrophysical scenarios, including rotating stars, stars with magnetic fields, and stars with a solid core. We also discuss the limitations of our analysis and possible avenues for further research.

Training effective grammatical error correction models for non-native languages is challenging due to the scarcity of high-quality annotated data. Furthermore, generalizing these models to new domains with limited data is difficult. To address this, we propose a method called Few-Shot Domain Adaptation via Meta-Learning for Grammatical Error Correction (FDAME). FDAME leverages a small amount of annotated data from a source domain to train a parametrized editor model. This model is optimized to minimize the discrepancy between the source and target domains. The editor model is then trained to correct sentences in the source domain, and the learned representation is used to correct sentences in the target domain. We evaluate FDAME on the WENGEC dataset and find that it outperforms a strong baseline in four domains with limited data. Additionally, FDAME demonstrates its versatility by adapting to new domains with different annotation styles. We also conduct an ablation study to analyze the components of FDAME and propose potential avenues for future research. The code for FDAME is available at https://github.com/THUSTARG/FDAME.

However, the rapidly changing market dynamics pose a challenge for policymakers seeking to design optimal ancillary services. This study proposes a novel framework, the Ancillary Services Acquisition Model, to analyze the interactions between generators, grid operators, and market participants. This model enables the assessment of various policy interventions, such as capacity mechanisms and renewable portfolio standards, and their impact on scheduling and dispatch decisions. By examining the effects of market dynamics on the value of ancillary services, this study highlights the importance of considering market interactions in policy design. Furthermore, the model's applicability is demonstrated through an empirical analysis of the German electricity market. This research contributes to the development of efficient scheduling and dispatch policies that balance the integration of renewable energy sources with the reliability of the power grid. This is particularly relevant for policymakers seeking to integrate high levels of renewable energy into their power grids. This study also provides a valuable tool for policymakers, enabling them to evaluate the effectiveness of various policy interventions in maintaining grid stability and promoting the integration of renewable energy sources. The Bayes factor method is a statistical tool used to compare the support of two competing hypotheses, X and Y, for some observed data D. The Bayes factor is calculated as the ratio of the probabilities of observing D under hypotheses X and Y, and is often determined through Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations. However, the Bayes factor can be sensitive to model assumptions and may not be robust in the presence of non-identifiability issues. In such cases, the Bayes factor may not accurately reflect the relative merits of the two hypotheses. This study proposes a novel approach to assess the Bayes factor's robustness by examining the distribution of Bayes factors obtained from MCMC simulations under different model formulations. Specifically, our method achieves superior performance in both monolingual and cross-lingual word similarity prediction tasks, as well as a significant improvement in the cross-lingual document classification task using word embeddings as features. Integrating visual and inertial sensors provides a robust and compact setup for estimating motion and reconstructing environments in various applications. However, the limited field-of-view and drift issues associated with inertial sensors necessitate efficient visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms to accurately estimate their transformation and 3D scene. To address this challenge, we propose a deep learning-based VIO framework called EMA-VIO that leverages external memory attention to effectively integrate visual and inertial data. The proposed network consists of a feature extraction module, an attention-based fusion module, a motion estimation module, and a 3D reconstruction module. The attention-based fusion module utilizes a novel attention mechanism to selectively incorporate visual and inertial features based on their reliability, as determined by an error map generated from the inertial measurement unit (IMU). The error map is updated at each time step to adapt to changing environments. The proposed EMA-VIO framework is evaluated on the TUM-VIO and TUM-VI datasets, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in terms of translation drift and 3D reconstruction accuracy. The proposed approach also exhibits robustness to various lighting conditions and outdoor scenarios. The code for EMA-VIO is available at https://github.com/zhengyin1995/EMA-VIO.

Our approach also enables the model to learn from just 0.5 labeled documents with partial annotations, specifically entity bounding boxes, which significantly reduces labeling costs. In this work, we develop a new algorithm to solve the rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-norm PCA problem, a well-known non-convex optimization problem. In its standard form, this problem assumes rotationally invariant symmetry, which significantly simplifies the problem to a single-dimensional optimization problem. In practice, this problem arises in various applications, such as subspace clustering and robust PCA with a non-convex formulation, where the data points are assumed to reside on the surface of a hypersphere. We design a linearly convergent first-order algorithm to solve this problem, leveraging the rotationally invariant symmetry to reduce the problem to a one-dimensional optimization problem along the geodesic surface of the hypersphere. We demonstrate the convergence of our algorithm and provide a convergence rate of $O(1/k)$ for its objective function value, as well as the recovery of the original data points with a rate of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}})$ in the space of probability measures. We also conduct numerical experiments to evaluate our algorithm's performance. We believe our algorithm's design can serve as a starting point for solving other rotationally invariant non-convex optimization problems. Mobile robots operating in unstructured environments require efficient navigation systems to effectively explore and move around. A key challenge in navigation is the representation of spatial knowledge, particularly when the environment is unfamiliar. Many mapping techniques rely on simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) to build a detailed, geometric representation of the environment, but these methods can be computationally expensive and prone to errors. In contrast, topological maps offer a more abstract representation of an environment's layout, allowing for efficient navigation, but may not accurately capture the details of an unknown space. To address this trade-off, we present a novel hierarchical topological map representation, HiTMap, which leverages a hybrid approach to balance the precision of geometric maps and the efficiency of topological representations. By utilizing a grid-based occupancy map to guide the navigation process and a topological map to structure the exploration, HiTMap enables a robot to efficiently explore an unknown environment while maintaining a clear understanding of its surroundings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HiTMap through simulation and real-world experiments, showcasing its ability to accurately navigate complex spaces with minimal computational requirements. source-target alignment, yet it often struggles to capture long-distance dependencies
relevant to prediction. This issue is exacerbated when the target sequence is
lengthy, leading to poor performance in the latter parts of the output. To address
this limitation, we introduce a novel look-ahead attention mechanism that suppresses
irrelevant distant information towards the end of the target sequence. This is
accomplished by computing two separate attention weights for the initial and final
parts of the target sequence, which are then combined to guide the decoder. Our
experiments on four large public datasets demonstrate that our look-ahead attention
outperforms the standard attention mechanism and other baselines, particularly in

In recent years, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have gained significant popularity for processing complex graph data, and various GCNN architectures have demonstrated superior performance in numerous applications. However, the underlying principles of GCNNs lack a clear intuitive explanation, hindering the development of novel designs and efficient training methods. This paper proposes a new perspective on GCNNs by drawing an analogy to matched filtering in signal processing, and we term this approach the "Intuitive Matched Filtering" (IMF) theory. The IMF framework provides a clear and concise explanation of GCNNs, including the reasons behind their robustness to noisy data and the effectiveness of skip connections. Furthermore, the IMF theory offers practical insights into designing GCNNs, including the optimal choice of graph convolution layers and the application of graph attention networks. The IMF theory is supported by numerical experiments and can be applied to various GCNN architectures, including Graph Convolutional Networks, Graph Attention Network, and Graph Neural Network, among others. The IMF framework paves the way for a deeper understanding of GCNNs and facilitates the development of novel GCNN designs and efficient training methods. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by breaking them down into smaller components. This hierarchical approach is characterized by a high-level decision made at the grid's level, followed by a series of lower-level decisions made at the individual cell level. We develop an algorithm to determine an optimal hierarchical policy and demonstrate that it leads to a significant reduction in the complexity of the decision-making process. Furthermore, we establish that the value function can be represented as the sum of two separate value functions corresponding to the two levels of the hierarchy. We also introduce a new performance metric to evaluate hierarchical policies and utilize it to show that the best hierarchical policy is equivalent to the optimal baseline policy in terms of value, albeit with a larger gap compared to the non-hierarchical case. We round out the study by providing a hierarchical solution method for the standard 3x3 grid world. Our research offers a fresh perspective on the application of hierarchical methods in solving large-scale stochastic games. We also discuss the limitations of our approach and potential avenues for improvement. We make our code publicly available.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, a significant challenge is addressing the issue of interference, where a policy that excels at one task struggles with another due to limited shared state space. This problem is particularly pronounced in model-based methods where the policy is trained using the same world model across multiple tasks. To overcome this limitation, we developed a novel approach that employs a separate, shared dynamics model to generate a set of augmented state variables, allowing the policy to be trained independently for each task while reducing interference. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in both single-shot and online multi-task learning settings, achieving superior performance to comparable baselines. Our approach also offers a significant computational advantage, as training a policy for each task in isolation is generally more efficient than training a single policy that can handle multiple tasks. To further validate our approach, we conducted a series of ablation studies to isolate the contributing factors of our method's success. Our method's simplicity and efficiency make it an attractive option for a wide range of applications, including multi-task learning with continuous action spaces and model-based policy optimization under limited data. We have made our code publicly available for the research community.

In 1931, Kurt Godel established the first of several incompleteness theorems for formal systems like Peano Arithmetic (PA), demonstrating that within any consistent, arithmetically-sound first-order theory like PA, a paradox arises when attempting to prove the consistency of the system itself. To address this challenge, a novel model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet has been developed to capture both short-term and long-term audio patterns by incorporating a pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural network. Experimental results demonstrate Quasi-Periodic WaveNet's superiority over WaveNet in generating music with long-term patterns, and its ability to produce high-quality speech and music samples. Furthermore, the model's efficiency has been proven by achieving comparable performance to WaveNet at a significantly lower computational cost. In this study, we focus on chest X-rays and create a new dataset with 1,000 images, each containing five different types of manipulations. We then train a series of models to detect these manipulations and evaluate their performance. Furthermore, we explore the potential of these models to detect whether an image has been altered to deceive a deep learning-based COVID-19 diagnosis system. Our findings demonstrate that it's possible to develop models capable of detecting various types of image alterations, including those designed to deceive a deep learning-based COVID-19 diagnosis system. We also examine the impact of these manipulations on the accuracy of the diagnosis system and propose a method to estimate the likelihood of an image being altered to deceive the system. Our research provides a foundation for developing tools that can detect manipulated chest X-rays and highlights the importance of incorporating disease-aware image editing into medical imaging analysis systems. Our dataset and code are available for public use.
